gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Counter-Strike 2 kicks players on Valve Official Servers for hardware input automation such as Snap Tap / SOCD, so of the features these under-$50 boards advertise for 'Valorant and CS2', only rapid trigger and adjustable actuation are usable in CS2 matchmaking.
standout_why: Compared against the three rival pages I could read. mechanicalkeyboard.net's HE68 Lite review (cited) lists 'SOCD (Snap Key)' as a feature and says only 'how SOCD inputs are treated varies by game', without naming CS2, Valve or the kick. hlplanet's guide (cited) mentions Snap Tap as a feature with no restriction. PC Gamer's guide (cited) returned only navigation to my fetch, so I could not check it; PC Gamer covered the ban in a separate 2024 news story, so its guide may mention it. The rivals therefore have part of it (SOCD is game-dependent) but not the rule itself. The two mechanism findings that would have scored higher (the NS68 tri-mode's polling rate per connection mode, and magnet-polarity limits on 'hot-swappable') could not be sourced: gamakay.com returned HTTP 429 on all five attempts and the switch-maker pages were blocked.
decides: It confirms rather than changes the pick. A CS2 buyer should choose on rapid trigger step, polling/scan rate and switch, and should not pay for or rely on Snap Tap / SOCD; the feature has to be switched off before a match. It does not separate the under-$50 boards from each other. The mechanism that would separate our in-budget row (Gamakay NS68, wired $36.79 vs tri-mode $39.99 per the brief's 2026-11-21 partner read) from the wired-only Epomaker HE68 Lite is whether the NS68 keeps 8,000 Hz and rapid trigger on 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth. That is unsourced here and must be read from Gamakay's page before the page claims anything about the tri-mode variant. hlplanet already calls the NS68 the cheapest wireless option without stating its wireless polling rate.

findings.label: Valve's CS2 rule on input automation (Snap Tap / SOCD class features)
findings.value: Valve: "We are no longer going to allow automation (via scripting or hardware) that circumvent these core skills"; "players suspected of automating multiple player actions from a single game input may be kicked from their match" (initially exclusively on Valve Official Servers)
findings.source_title: Valve bans keyboard automation in Counter-Strike 2 update (GamingOnLinux, 21 Aug 2024)
findings.note: Valve's words as quoted by GamingOnLinux. Valve's original post (https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/730/view/6500469346429600836) failed to open with a certificate error, so it is not the source. The penalty is a kick from the match, not a ban. The rule dates from August 2024; I did not verify it is unchanged in November 2026.

findings.label: Valve's instruction to owners of keyboards with the feature
findings.value: "If you have a keyboard that includes an input-automation feature" ... "be sure to disable the feature before you join a match"
findings.source_title: Valve bans keyboard automation in Counter-Strike 2 update (GamingOnLinux, 21 Aug 2024)
findings.note: Valve's words as quoted by GamingOnLinux. The article says Valve named no hardware maker; 'Snap Tap Mode' appears only as an example of such a feature.

findings.label: Why Valve drew the line at hardware
findings.value: "Recently, some hardware features have blurred the line between manual input and automation"
findings.source_title: Valve bans keyboard automation in Counter-Strike 2 update (GamingOnLinux, 21 Aug 2024)
findings.note: The same post also disables in-game binds that combine more than one movement and/or attack action (null binds, jump-throw binds). Rapid trigger sends one action per input and is not described as automation in the quoted text.

findings.label: What the cited rival says about SOCD
findings.value: "SOCD (Snap Key) prioritises the latest keypress of opposite direction keys"; "Note that how SOCD inputs are treated varies by game."
findings.source_title: Epomaker HE68 Lite Review 2026: Best $50 Hall Effect Keyboard? (mechanicalkeyboard.net)
findings.note: Confirms the HE68 Lite ships an SOCD feature. The review does not name CS2 or Valve's kick; this is the partial overlap behind the standout score of 1.

findings.label: Connection and switch limits as the cited rival states them
findings.value: "Wired only (no Bluetooth or 2.4GHz wireless)"; "hot-swappable with other magnetic switches but not compatible with standard MX mechanical switches"; 8,000 Hz polling and 128 kHz per-key scan rate "according to manufacturer specifications"
findings.source_title: Epomaker HE68 Lite Review 2026: Best $50 Hall Effect Keyboard? (mechanicalkeyboard.net)
findings.note: Reviewer's restatement of Epomaker's specs; no measured latency is given. The review notes 0.125 ms is the polling interval, not end-to-end latency. It quotes $49.99 from Epomaker's page on the review's own date, which is not a price read today.

findings.label: What the cited rival says about wireless latency and hot-swap
findings.value: "A 2.4 GHz dongle typically adds 20–100% latency"; "Bluetooth adds far more — it can turn 1 ms into 10 ms."; "Also every HE keyboard is hotswappable."
findings.source_title: Best Keyboards w/ Hall Effect magnetic switches [2026 GUIDE] (HLPlanet)
findings.note: HLPlanet's generalisations, not measurements of a named board. It gives no per-mode polling figure for any under-$50 board and does not cover magnet polarity. Its one compatibility note concerns a Gateron KS-37 board that does not take Gateron Jade or White switches.

findings.label: How the cited rival positions the NS68
findings.value: "If you need wireless, the Gamakay NS68 at $42.99 is the cheapest option."; table note: "Wired or wireless, extremely cheap."
findings.source_title: Best Keyboards w/ Hall Effect magnetic switches [2026 GUIDE] (HLPlanet)
findings.note: $42.99 is HLPlanet's figure on its own date (page dated 2026-10-26), not a price read today. HLPlanet states no polling rate for the NS68's 2.4 GHz or Bluetooth modes; that is the open gap.

unsourced: Gamakay NS68 polling rate, scan rate and rapid-trigger availability per connection mode (wired, 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth), and what differs between the wired and tri-mode variants. gamakay.com returned HTTP 429 on five attempts (storecheck.py three times, WebFetch on the US and en-mx product pages). An unopened Newegg listing in search results mentioned a 1K wireless polling rate for the NS68; treat that as a lead only.
Gamakay NS68 compatible magnetic switches, magnet orientation, sensor type, and whether its driver is a web app needing a WebHID browser (same 429 block; no manual or spec PDF was reached).

Why a 'hot-swappable' Hall effect board accepts only some magnetic switches (magnet pole orientation and flux range), in a maker's or named reviewer's words. Gateron's Jade page returned 403, the RTINGS Test Bench 1.4.2 changelog and the GamesRadar article returned no body text, and Pulsar's support article failed with a certificate error. Search snippets pointed to N-pole-down versus S-pole designs and flux range, but no page was opened.
Valve's original post, to quote directly and confirm the rule's current status; store.steampowered.com and counter-strike.net did not return the text.
Riot's position on Snap Tap / SOCD in Valorant; not searched within the call budget.

PC Gamer's NS68 review and its best Hall effect keyboards guide (reviewer name, score, wired vs wireless notes, any latency figure); both returned only navigation, including on a second try with an offset.

Whether the MCHOSE Ace 60 Pro, Aula WIN60 HE, Aula WIN68 HE and Redragon K617 HE ship an SOCD / Snap Tap feature, and their connection modes and compatible switches; no maker page was opened within the call budget.
Today's prices for the rival boards; none read (this angle did not reach the maker stores, and local curl was not permitted).
